faq.q: Why does lightning hit the lightning rod?
faq.a: Lightning tends to strike the tallest, most pointed conductor nearby. The metal rod sits on the highest point, so the strike is far more likely to hit it than the roof.
asks: Does a lightning rod attract lightning?

faq.q: Why is the cable from a lightning rod so thick?
faq.a: A lightning strike carries tens of thousands of amps for a split second. A thick copper or aluminium strip has very low resistance, so it carries that current without melting or sparking.
asks: What is the lightning conductor made of?

faq.a: It is a long copper rod driven deep into the ground at the bottom of the cable. It gives the current a wide, easy path into the soil.
asks: What is at the bottom of a lightning conductor?

faq.q: Where does the lightning go after it hits the ground?
faq.a: The charge spreads out through the damp soil and is absorbed by the Earth, which is so enormous that it soaks up the charge easily.
asks: What happens to the electricity from lightning?

faq.q: What happens to a building without a lightning rod?
faq.a: Lightning may hit the roof and force its way through brick, wood or wiring, which resist it. The huge current heats them, causing fires, bursts of steam in damp materials and smashed masonry.
asks: Why do tall buildings need lightning rods?

facts: Benjamin Franklin invented the lightning rod in the 1750s.
A typical lightning strike carries around 30,000 amps, for only a fraction of a second.
